t: Count the Number of Houses at a Certain Distance I
o: Houses 1..n form a path, plus one extra edge between x and y (possibly a self-loop, creating a cycle). For each distance k count ordered pairs at shortest-path distance exactly k. With n ≤ 100, BFS from every house — O(n²) total — is perfectly fine.
k: Graph = path 1–2–…–n plus edge (x, y); shortest distances need BFS since the extra edge creates a cycle.
Count ordered pairs: for each source, each other node contributes 1 to result[dist].
Self-loop x = y simply adds nothing new.

a.i: Run BFS from each of the n sources on the path+extra-edge graph, tallying distances into the result array. Total work O(n·(n+m)) = O(n²), well within limits.
s: Build adjacency: i↔i+1 for all i, plus x↔y (skip if x == y).
For each source s, BFS recording dist[].
a.t: O(n²) — n BFS traversals over an O(n)-edge graph
a.sp: O(n) — adjacency and distance arrays per BFS

a.i: Without BFS, the distance between houses a < b is min(b − a, |a − x| + 1 + |y − b|, |a − y| + 1 + |x − b|) — straight along the path or detouring through the extra edge in either direction. Evaluate all O(n²) pairs directly; equally fast here and avoids queue machinery.
s: For each ordered pair (a, b): d = min(b−a, |a−x|+1+|y−b|, |a−y|+1+|x−b|).
a.t: O(n²) — direct evaluation of every ordered pair

w: BFS-from-every-node is the safest general technique and extends naturally to the harder version with larger n (where you'd switch to counting via prefix sums over the cycle/path structure). Pitfall: convert between 1-indexed houses and 0-indexed arrays carefully, and handle x == y (self-loop adds no edge).
